body_markdown:
# Introduction

A tense helps show when an action happens and how the speaker views that action. English learning commonly groups tense forms into three time areas: present, past and future. Each area has four forms: simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous.

The chart below is a learning framework. Real English also uses context, time expressions and forms such as *going to* to talk about the future.

## The 12 tense forms

| Time | Form | Example |
|---|---|---|
| Present | Simple | I work every day. |
| Present | Continuous | I am working now. |
| Present | Perfect | I have finished the task. |
| Present | Perfect Continuous | I have been working for two hours. |
| Past | Simple | I worked yesterday. |
| Past | Continuous | I was working at 8 p.m. |
| Past | Perfect | I had finished before he arrived. |
| Past | Perfect Continuous | I had been working for two hours before the break. |
| Future | Simple | I will work tomorrow. |
| Future | Continuous | I will be working at 8 p.m. |
| Future | Perfect | I will have finished by Friday. |
| Future | Perfect Continuous | By noon, I will have been working for four hours. |

## Understand the four forms

### 1. Simple

Use the simple form for habits, facts, completed past events or future decisions and predictions.

- Present: She checks the register every morning.
- Past: She checked the register yesterday.
- Future: She will check it tomorrow.

### 2. Continuous

Use the continuous form to focus on an action in progress at a particular time.

- Present: They are waiting outside.
- Past: They were waiting when the bus arrived.
- Future: They will be waiting at the entrance.

### 3. Perfect

The perfect form connects an action to a reference time. The present perfect often connects a past action to the present; the past perfect places one past event before another; the future perfect looks back from a future point.

- Present: I have sent the email.
- Past: I had sent the email before the meeting.
- Future: I will have sent it by 5 p.m.

### 4. Perfect continuous

This form highlights the duration or ongoing nature of an activity up to a reference time.

- Present: He has been studying for an hour.
- Past: He had been studying for an hour before dinner.
- Future: He will have been studying for an hour by 7 p.m.

## Common mistakes

- Incorrect: She go to work every day. Correct: She goes to work every day.
- Incorrect: I am knowing him. Correct: I know him. Many state verbs, such as *know* and *believe*, are not normally used in continuous forms.
- Incorrect: I have seen him yesterday. Correct: I saw him yesterday. Use the past simple with a finished time such as *yesterday*.
- Incorrect: I am working here since Monday. Correct: I have been working here since Monday.

## Practice

Choose the correct form.

1. He ___ to the office every day. (go / goes)
2. They ___ dinner now. (are having / have)
3. I ___ the report yesterday. (finish / finished)
4. She ___ already left. (has / have)
5. We ___ for an hour. (have been waiting / are wait)
6. By next week, he ___ the course. (will complete / will have completed)

## Answers

1. goes: third-person singular in the present simple.
2. are having: an action happening now.
3. finished: a completed past event.
4. has: use *has* with she.
5. have been waiting: duration continuing up to now.
6. will have completed: completion before a future deadline.

## A practical way to learn tenses

Choose one verb, such as *work*. Make one sentence in each tense form and connect it to your real routine. Practise the same sentences aloud on different days. Understanding the meaning is more useful than memorising a chart without context.

faq.question: How many English tenses are commonly taught?
faq.answer: Learners are commonly taught 12 forms, combining present, past and future with simple, continuous, perfect and perfect continuous.

faq.question: Do I need to memorise all 12 forms at once?
faq.answer: No. Learn one time area and one form at a time, using meaningful examples.

faq.question: What is the difference between simple and continuous?
faq.answer: Simple forms commonly express habits, facts or events; continuous forms highlight an activity in progress.
